memories.memory_text: I told Jonah Arden I panicked when the girl wanted me to kiss her—I didn't know how to move my head, whether to close my eyes, or how much tongue to use, and I even asked him what if I pitch a tent, because I was so nervous about losing control.

memories.memory_text: I tried to copy Jonah Arden's moves, flashing that goofy smile he told me to use, and then I saw Muffy mime puking—right at me—like I was something disgusting she couldn't even stomach.

I opened the door and there he was—covered in mud, tiny again, like some nightmare version of my past, and I just screamed and slammed it shut, wobbling away in my stupid robe with tissues stuck to my toes.
I chucked the toaster into the hot tub, thinking this crazy idea might actually fix Jonah Arden—then he screamed and nothing happened, so I realized the damn thing wasn't even plugged in.
I was crouched there, reaching to plug the cord back in, when I asked Jonah Arden what he was even doing by the river—right before he suddenly freaked out and bolted.

I was researching the spell online, trying to make sense of it, when Jonah Arden walked in and dropped this insane bomb that he’s going back to high school—like, actually enrolling. I thought he was joking at first, but then he just grabbed a beer like it was the most normal thing in the world.

I snatched the beer right out of Jonah Arden’s hand and chugged it—I don’t even know why, it just felt like the only way to react without screaming. Then I told him straight: I’m not going back to Fitch High, no way, and he better not drag me into this mess.

I told Jonah Arden to flunk his classes or start a fight so I could play the helpless Nico Dalton and get another shot at seeing the Reese North—she’s smart, which is honestly her only flaw as far as I’m concerned.
Some lady told me I should be reported to child services and I just told her to mind her own business—like she knows anything about raising a kid in crisis.
I burst into Jonah Arden's room covered in seaweed, joking that I was detoxing and slimming down my problem areas—couldn't help but play it up, even if I looked ridiculous.
I tossed Jonah Arden the keys and said, 'That ought'a put you over the top'—he lit up like a kid on Christmas, and I felt that flicker of pride, like I was actually helping him become someone new.

I was just floating there, drink in hand, and then Morgan Carver showed up out of nowhere, tossing divorce papers on the table like it was nothing. I remember the envelope hitting the wood with a dull slap, and me saying it out loud—'That envelope contains divorce papers'—like if I said it, it’d feel real.

After Jonah Arden saw the envelope and just stood there silent, I snapped—brought up the college apps I found in his room, how he’s just gonna skip off while I’m stuck here. When he tried to walk away, I yelled, 'I’m not paying for college!'—and even as the words left my mouth, I knew it was too much, but I couldn’t take it back.

I burst in yelling 'Way to go, slugger!' and called Jonah Arden a wuss for the black eye—then sat between him and Avery Arden, flashing my teeth and blowing in Jonah Arden's face just to lighten the mood.
I told Morgan Carver I sent the divorce papers and promised I’d tell him to call home if I heard from him—she looked like she was falling apart, and I couldn’t bring myself to say more.
I said 'It's Nico Dalton. I mean Nico Dalton. Not your Nico Dalton. My Nico Dalton,' and immediately wished I could take it back—why did I let that slip in front of Avery Arden?

I stepped out in those tight clothes, checked my ass in the mirror, and said it loud—'Baby's got back.' Felt stupid, maybe, but also kind of proud. Reese North was gonna see me like this, and for once, I wasn’t just the Nico Dalton no one listens to.

Jonah Arden asked if he could have a party, and I said no—Reese North’s coming over, and I didn’t want a mess. He twisted my nipple, I twisted his back. We both yelled, held on a second, then let go when people stared. I forced a smile and walked away.

I remember standing inside, feeling the bass shake the walls while kids I barely knew poured into my house like it was some kind of zoo—I didn’t even have time to process it before the whole place exploded.
I handed the hostess a fifty and told her to put it toward her studies, then ordered a $2000 bottle of wine, thinking Reese North would be impressed.
Reese North threw her napkin down and called me disgusting, said I cared more about showing off my money than about Jonah Arden—then I realized I’d messed up and grabbed her wrist, apologizing.

I told Reese North about wearing a full wizard costume everywhere, even to high school, and how I never got a date—then she laughed, and I felt exposed but weirdly proud, like maybe being a nerd wasn’t something to hide.

She called herself an elf princess, I played along as Marius the wizard, and for a second—after we both shouted 'Level 10. Mage. Level 15. Bitch!'—we just stared, breathless, and I swear the air between us crackled; then I panicked and yelled for the check.

I was just joking around with Reese North about the Russian mafia, and then we turned the corner and saw my house—kids everywhere, trampling the lawn, some guy pissing in the flower bed—and I remember thinking, that little bastard’s dead, I’m gonna kill him.
I stormed up the driveway, Reese North right behind me, and the next thing I know some kid yells 'It's Reese North!'—then they all freak out and scatter like I busted a rave.
I screamed 'Everybody out!' at the top of my lungs, but no one even looked my way—like I was invisible or something.

I knocked and knocked, my knuckles probably raw by now—two days is long enough for anyone to hide, even Jonah Arden. When I finally heard that dragging sound and the click, I just turned the knob and walked in.
I asked Jonah Arden if he was alright, sitting there on his bed while he groaned under the covers—couldn’t even face the light.
I showed him the divorce papers, held them up like a damn receipt—then said mine with Reese North was lost, like it didn’t still sting.
I was speeding out of the driveway and lost control—tires screeching, the wheel jerking hard—then suddenly I was tearing across the neighbor's lawn before I could even react.

I remember screeching to a halt in my BMW, bolting out with Jonah Arden, sprinting up those courthouse steps—completely out of breath and not even sure what we were doing, just knowing we had to stop her.
I turned off the radio and told Jonah Arden the truth—he needed to let them go, really let them go—and when he looked at me like the world was ending, I knew it was the only thing left to say.
I remember asking Jonah Arden where he was going, and he just said he was moving on—like it was nothing—then got in the car and drove off without looking back.

relations.relation_summary: Nico Dalton and Jonah Arden share a complex, multifaceted relationship defined primarily by a confirmed father-son kinship, as repeatedly evidenced by Nico Dalton calling Jonah Arden 'son' and Jonah Arden addressing Nico Dalton as 'Nico Dalton'. This familial bond is interwoven with deep emotional intimacy, as both characters refer to each other as 'best friend' and 'buddies', and engage in casual, affectionate interactions such as nudging, whispering, and fist-bumping. They participate in cooperative events such as creating a MySpace page together, investigating supernatural occurrences, and physically intervening in shared crises, indicating a strong collaborative dynamic. However, their relationship is marked by intense emotional volatility, oscillating between camaraderie and violent hostility. They engage in physical altercations including wrestling, twisting each other's nipples, kneeing, and mutual threats, often escalating from emotional tension but ending with reconciliation—such as forcing smiles after a fight or continuing to interact as friends afterward. Despite Nico Dalton explicitly stating 'I hate you' and threatening Jonah Arden, these hostile moments are consistently framed within the context of their familial bond, suggesting that conflict is a mode of engagement rather than true estrangement. The relationship evolves cyclically, with cooperation and affection punctuated by bursts of aggression, yet they repeatedly return to collaboration, indicating resilience and deep interdependence. This dynamic significantly influences their behavior, as they consistently seek each other out in moments of need, act as emotional confidants, and jointly pursue goals despite their volatility.

The relationship between Nico Dalton and Reese North is complex and marked by conflicting dynamics. Initially, there is evidence of a romantic interest, as Nico Dalton states that Reese North has agreed to go out with him, suggesting a potential intimate connection. However, this is contrasted by Reese North's explicit denial of the meeting being a date, indicating ambiguity or misalignment in how each perceives the relationship. Their interactions are increasingly defined by hostility, with Reese North expressing disgust toward Westhaven Hospital behavior, particularly his materialism and disrespectful comments about others like Jonah Arden. She directly criticizes his transformation from marginalized to wealthy, resenting his perceived moral decline and prioritization of wealth over authentic relationships. This clash of values manifests in emotionally charged confrontations, such as when Nico Dalton makes provocative remarks and Reese North responds by throwing her napkin or ushering him to the door and shutting it. Key events underscore the deterioration of their rapport: Nico Dalton physically restrains Reese North by taking her wrist, an act of control that precedes his apology, suggesting awareness of his transgressions. His apology indicates a desire for reconciliation, but Reese North's decisive action of closing the door on him demonstrates rejection and a boundary being enforced. The relationship evolves from tentative romantic possibility to one defined by antagonism and disillusionment, with Reese North withdrawing emotionally and physically. These dynamics influence both characters' behaviors—Nico Dalton oscillates between pursuit and remorse, while Reese North becomes increasingly resistant and dismissive, signaling the collapse of any meaningful connection.

memories.memory_text: I stopped the photo from starting because Nico Dalton wasn't there yet—didn't matter what Adrian Warren said, he was part of the team.
Reese Adler said the scouts were already watching and I could play anywhere if I kept it up—felt like everything was clicking that morning.
I ran after her, called out 'Morgan Carver! Wait,' and when she stopped, I kissed her—felt her against the wall, didn't think, just moved.
I stood in front of the mirror, straightened my tie, and told myself today was going to be good—like I do every morning. Then I yanked the tie up hard, like I was choking myself with it.
I straightened my tie and buttoned my jacket, ready to stand up when Roger said my name—then I heard 'Wendy' and just collapsed back into the chair, stunned.
I confronted Roger after the meeting, asking how he could pass me over after 18 years—Wendy’s only been here two months—and he just shrugged it off because she has a college degree.

I was staring at that old team photo, at my younger self—so sure of everything—and it hit me how fast it all vanished. I said out loud, 'I had life by the the black photograph in that picture. Everything was possible. Then a few minutes later, pffffft, all gone.'

The Skyler Quincy called me 'Jonah Arden'—a name nobody uses—and said, 'You never know who's listening,' then disappeared. When I turned back, he was just... gone. I started to ask how he knew my name, but then Avery Arden interrupted.
I asked her if she was okay after she said she got into Georgetown, and she told me I wouldn't understand—like I wasn't even there.

I pulled up behind the nursery van, asked if your mom was home, and tried to make it light with the barbecue plan—but Avery Arden shot me a look and said we only see them once a week. I felt it hit hard, like I’d been punched in the gut before I even got inside.
The thunder cracked so loud it felt like the car shook, and I nearly jumped out of my skin—Jesus!—then the rain came down all at once, hammering the windshield like it was trying to get in.
I saw him—just standing there in the storm, leaning over the railing—and before I even thought, I slammed on the brakes and threw the door open, jumping out into the downpour.

I stood there covered in mud, my suit hanging off me, and when Nico Dalton opened the door I could see the fear in his eyes before he even said a word. I told him I'd had a really rough night, but he just screamed and slammed the door.
I saw my face in the mirror—mud washed off and I was still seventeen, staring back at me like it wasn't even real. I screamed, but the reflection didn't change.

I tore off my jacket and shirt, saw my hairless chest, then yanked down my pants to check—still seventeen everywhere. I grabbed Nico Dalton, desperate, and begged him to do something, to pinch me, anything.
I was in the hot tub, soaked in that gross green water, and when Nico Dalton asked what I was doing by the river, it hit me—*the Skyler Quincy* was there that day, same as me.

I showed the Skyler Quincy the 1989 photo, pointing to myself, asking if he remembered me, but she just looked at it like it was ancient history and said, 'That picture's from 1989,' like I was stupid for even asking.
I walked in, turned on the sink, and heard someone ask for help. I looked and saw underwear caught on the stall door. I opened it and found Avery Arden hanging there, his feet off the ground.
After I got him down and he fixed himself, he asked how I knew his name, and when I lied about being Jonah Arden, he didn’t recognize me—even said he wasn’t one of them, like I thought he was.
I told Nico Dalton I'm going back to high school—just like that, no warning. I could see he thought I'd lost it, but I had to do it. My kids need me, and that's all that matters.
Nico Dalton asked what I'd tell Morgan Carver, and I said nothing. I don't know how she'll take it, but I can't face her. I just have to vanish, even if it feels wrong.

I walked into the cafeteria smiling, trying to play it cool, but the second that kid yelled 'Go Hot Pants!' everyone turned and started laughing—phones out, all watching that damn fire dance video. I could feel my face burning as I passed table after table, hoping Terry Marlowe would at least look at me.

I just stood there while Graham Wilder took my hat, scooped ice cream from Terry Marlowe's tray, and smashed it right on my head—cold, sticky, dripping down my neck—everyone watching, nobody saying a word. I didn’t even look at Terry Marlowe when I turned to walk out.

I sat there with a pink Shirley Temple in front of me, plucking a cherry off the stem, knowing I couldn't go back to that school after everything—the fire, the videos, the mocking, mint chip in my ears.

I watched the screen as Nico Dalton filled my MySpace friends with nothing but hot girls, photoshopped me in places I’d never been, and listed bands and movies I’d never heard of—this fake version of me looked like some cool, untouchable guy.
I sat down across from Avery Arden at lunch, just like that—no big deal. But when I mentioned meeting his mom, he froze, and so did I. I didn’t even realize I’d said it until he pointed it out.
Before I left, I told him I’d swing by around seven. Just like that—plans made. I don’t know why it felt right, but it did.
I told Morgan Carver my mom was a convict—B&E, shanking, parole—she died after I warned her about kite surfing in a hurricane. Then I tried to laugh it off by asking if she was dating Adrian Warren.

She kept staring at me, not saying anything, and then said I looked just like her late husband as a teenager. I didn't know what to do, so I pointed at her dirty clothes and asked if she was gardening.

I saw the envelope on the table and realized Morgan Carver had left the divorce papers—then Nico Dalton threw it in my face that he found my college applications, like I’d betrayed him just for trying to make something of myself.
I tossed Avery Arden the ball and told him to show me what he got—then saw that spark in his eyes when he started dribbling, quick and low, like he finally believed he could do this.
I saw Graham Wilder's elbow snap back and Avery Arden drop like a sack—then I didn't think, I just charged, tackled him hard, and the world went red.
I stared out the window, trying to hold it together when Nico Dalton said I needed to let them go—my family—and something inside me just broke, because I knew he was right.
I plugged my the blue case into the laptop and pulled those photos off—just in case I ever needed to remember who I was back then.
I typed the email fast, didn't look back—just hit send with some fake name, like it wasn't really me saying goodbye.
I was draining shot after shot, just me and the net, when Reese Adler came in and told me college scouts were coming to watch me play tonight—he said I could play anywhere if I kept it up.

September 7th, 1988 was the first
time I saw you. You were reading
`The Great Gatsby' and wearing a
Guns N Roses T-shirt. I'd never
seen anything so perfect. I
remember thinking I had to have you
or I'd die...not in a psycho kinda
way but in that beautiful,
innocent, unaffected way that way
only a 17 year-old kid can have.
I had life by the the black photograph in that picture. Everything was possible. Then a few minutes later, pffffft, all gone.
Mouth is alive, with juices like wine, and I'm hungry like the wolf
My son was hanging by his underwear from a bathroom stall door and my daughter was being mauled by a smarmy gorilla. They need me.
Don't you walk away from me, Terry Marlowe!
It was incredible! I was incredible! You should'a seen me! I humiliated Graham Wilder in front of the entire lunchroom. Everyone was clapping. The popular girls were begging to give me their numbers!
Nico Dalton, I can't help you with the girls if you keep showing up places dressed like the Cookie Crisp guy. Okay? Dude, don't look now but I think Muffy Campanella is scopin' you hard.
Just introduce yourself. Then compliment her on something she never gets complimented on. Like if she has big, meaty, man hands tell her she should be a hand model.

Wow. 10 whole dollars. At that
rate I should be able to buy
tickets in...2011.
Your next word better be `cookies' or you're in big, big trouble!
Morgan Carver!
It's adultery! If this were Afghanistan she'd be dragged through the village by goats. You need to talk to her.

I warned her about kite surfing
during hurricane season. So how
are things with you? Doing
anything exciting? Dating?
Flirting with Adrian Warren maybe?
YYYYEEEEOOOOOWWWWWWW!!!

Today is going to be a good day. I
love my job. I am a lucky man.
Who's lucky? Jonah Arden.

memories.memory_text: Jonah Arden called me his girlfriend in front of everyone, right there on the bench, and I just smiled and said everything was fine—even though I felt my chest tighten and my hands go cold.
Adrian Warren smiled at me while dribbling past and said he was dedicating his first basket to me, and then I couldn't stay—I started walking out, feeling like I couldn't breathe.
I turned and leaned against the wall, and then Jonah Arden was there—his mouth on mine before I could say anything, before I even turned back around.
I felt the shovel bite into the dirt as I ripped out that dead shrub, and when Jonah Arden smirked and started singing that stupid song, I almost laughed—then caught myself and pushed him away.
After he tried to blame me with that silence, I threw the shovel down and said I never asked him to marry me—my voice cracked, but I made sure he heard the truth: he’s not the victim here.
I remember Jonah Arden telling me he was in Peru finding himself, but then Nico Dalton said he was detained at Guantanamo—something didn’t add up, and I wasn’t sure who was lying.
I opened the door, ready to greet him, and then I saw his face—my breath caught, I couldn't speak. He looks so much like... I don't know, it hit me all at once.

I stared at Jonah Arden, trying to make sense of his face—Nico Dalton’s son, he said, but he didn’t look like him at all. When he mentioned his mother was a convict, something about the way he looked at Dostoevsky’s book made my skin tighten.
He brought up Adrian Warren out of nowhere, casually, like he had a right to know. And the way he looked like my husband—like a younger version—froze me. I couldn’t look away, but I didn’t answer.
Jonah Arden called me 'Morgan Carver'—a name only my husband uses—and a chill ran up my spine before I could even respond.
I watched Jonah Arden walk back inside after Avery Arden called him, and I couldn't shake the unease about who he really was.
I tossed the manila envelope onto the patio table without looking at Jonah Arden, my voice steady even though my hands wouldn’t stop shaking.
I saw Avery Arden sitting there with his jaw clenched, and I had to ask—'Fighting? What's gotten into you?'—but then I saw how he winced, and all I could think was that he was hurt, my poor baby.

I crouched down to Jonah Arden, took the ice pack off his eye, and touched his face—'Ouch. You poor thing. Does it hurt?'—and when he said it didn't anymore, I felt him lean into it, but then he said I smelled great, and it made me pull back.
I told Jonah Arden gloves were for sissies, then caught myself blushing when he joked about wanting to help—immediately backtracked with the pay, offered ten, then twenty when he mocked the rate.
We lifted a roll of sod together, him making a joke about benefits, me offering a baloney sandwich—then we both laughed, and for a second it didn't feel like work or awkwardness, just easy.
I pressed the limestone into the sod beside Jonah Arden, feeling the damp grass give under the weight, both of us aligning the stones without speaking.
I handed the water bottles to the boys, and as I turned back toward the house, I felt eyes on me—Jonah Arden’s gaze, heavy and sudden, like a hand brushing my shoulder without permission.
I turned the hose on Jonah Arden while he was sleeping in the grass, then ran when he jumped up and came after me.
I felt Jonah Arden’s hand land on my leg, so I slid it off like it was nothing—just a casual brush, like dusting off a seat before sitting.
I turned and saw him standing there, just staring—I didn’t know how long he’d been watching me—and when he asked to zip me up, I told him I was wearing a sweater and shut the door in his face.
I flicked the switch and said 'Ta da!'—seeing the thousands of the wooden box fill the OASIS, I felt my chest tighten with hope, wanting Jonah Arden and Avery Arden to truly see what I built for us.
I remember the way Jonah Arden looked at the Westhaven Hospital, actually stunned, saying I was talented—really saying it like he meant it, not just polite words.
Avery Arden asked why I was dressed up, and it hit me—I had a date tonight. I almost forgot, but then I said it out loud, like it was real.
I pushed Jonah Arden aside and opened the door—Adrian Warren was standing there with flowers, and I just said, 'Don't mind him. You all set?' like nothing had happened.
After I opened the door, Adrian Warren said I looked ravishing, and I remember the way he looked at me—calm, sure—before I walked toward the van like I’d planned it all along.
I pushed through the crowd, heart pounding, calling for Avery Arden—then Jonah Arden said he was with his girlfriend, and all I could think was, Avery Arden has a girlfriend?
I told him about my guilt, about failing my marriage and not being the mother I should have been. I placed my hand over his and looked into his eyes. There was something familiar about him.
He kissed me—just lunged in—and I didn’t even process it until my hand moved on its own; the slap echoed, but the shock was worse, especially when he said he was my husband.
I stood there with my hand raised, saying 'Yes, Evan Calloway' and 'No, Evan Calloway,' feeling the weight of it all when he wasn't even there to face it.
I stood there frozen, listening to him read words that sounded like us—our beginning—words I thought only I remembered, and I couldn’t stop the tears from falling.
I reached for the paper after he left, needing to hold what he’d read, and when I saw it was just courthouse directions, I didn’t understand—my hands just went still.

I was working at the kitchen table when Jonah Arden’s email came in—clicked on the link he sent, and there it was: 'Morgan Carver’s Sanctuaries.' I remember the name on the screen, clear and bold, and I couldn’t help but smile.
I saw Jonah Arden at the other end of the tunnel, and when I asked what took him so long, he didn't answer—just pulled me into his arms.
After we kissed, he took my hand and said we shouldn't tell the kids—especially Terry Marlowe—about us, and I didn't say no.
